Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, I was directing attention to the conduct of the Treasury Board at the time the certificate was granted. We have Mr. McCarthy's letter and the minister's answer requesting particulars of the charges against these men who were asking a certificate for the Farmers' Bank, and the minister promised that the matter would be considered by the Treasury Board. All particulars were furnished, the charges were made against the promoters of the bank and yet the Treasury Board met on November 30, but the papers and particulars which had been furnished at the request of the minister had been returned to Mr. McCarthy on November 7. Evidently these men got the certificate without the objections having been considered by the Treasury Board. It is peculiar that the Treasury Board met on November 30 and that on that day there was correspondence between the Minister of Finance and Mr. Travers, and that on that day Mr. Travers received his certificate for the bank to start business. It looks as if everything had been hurried on that day. There was no occasion for hurry, an extension had been granted, good until January 18, so there were still about six weeks before the charter would expire. Who was nurrying the Treasury Board and the Finance Minister? The question arises, was Mr. Calvert or the president of the Trust and Guarantee Company hurrying matters on, and if so for what reason? Was there something in it for these men? These questions naturally arise, and the people out in the couofry are asking them.
There is something very distressing in the failure of the Farmers' Bank. Members from constituencies which were very much affected, receive many letters about it. I receive letters every few days appealing to me and asking if the government and the right hon. First Minister will not do something to relieve those who have
been robbed of their all, for there are many whose whole substance has been taken from them by this, and wanting to know if there is not some relief to be granted by the government. If the government had been as careful of the people's interest as they should be, then immediately this failure occurred, they would have done something to relieve the situation and Ito show the people that they wanted to get after these designing men who robbed the shareholders and depositors. I know the plea is put up that there is no law to touch these men, that the government had no power to interfere. Is that so? Has it come to this? I am perfectly well aware they say there was a law and that the law was being enforced in Toronto, but we know how comparatively helpless that is; we know how the majority of these men have escaped the hands of justice and how the great offender in the case received what everybody says is too light a sentence, only six years for the crime he had perpetrated. The impression is abroad that he should have had 26 years. It looks as if there was something lax in the law when a man guilty of such a crime should receive a sentence of only six years, and is to-day living comparatively a gentleman giving evidence in Toronto. It looks as. if the government ought to have done something more to get after those fellows. If there is no law to get after them should there not be? Are designing men to be allowed to rob innocent men, women and children of their hard-earned savings? If so, God help Canada and help her legislators, her lawmakers to make laws that will get after such men quickly.
There were warnings without number in connection with this bank failure. We had first of all numerous personal appeals made not only to the Finance Minister, but to other members of the government. These were more than gossip, they were practically definite -charges made- against the promoters of this bank, for the way in which they were trying to get the bank started. Then there was the direct charge made by Mr. Leighton McCarthy, coming from shareholders who had been, to say the least, fooled, who were being robbed and misrepresented in connection with the floating of this bank, and on the very day that the Treasury Board issued that certificate we have Mr. Clouston, in the name of the Canadian Bankers' Association, protesting strongly -against that certificate being issued. Then within four months of the bank starting business we have this protest from the manager of the Milton branch of the bank, saying there was crookedness in connection with the management at head office, and we had later on another appeal from the Canadian Bankers' Association, through its secretary, saying there was something crooked in connection with the doings of

this bank. All these warnings about the misdoings of the management should have shown it was time to do something. Had steps been taken by the department in some way to arrest these men in their work of robbing these innocent people, something could have been done. I do not wish te take time to recite the particulars of that insurance matter in New York state. You will remember that when the Minister of Finance was appealed to, his one answer was that contained in a letter dated January 12, 1910, to Wm. H. Hotchkiss, Superintendent of Insurance, Albany, New York:
There bang no government bank inspection in Canada' I do not see bow we can at present take the action that you desire. Probably the bank on application from you would explain the whole matter.
(Signed) W. S. FIELDING.
Now, if there is not government bank inspection in Canada which would prevent these abuses, whose fault is it? Ought there not to be some way by which banks can be controlled, and some way in which bank managers can be prevented from fleecing the people. Let me refer briefly to the question of bank inspection. At different times the subject has been discussed in this House, but no action has up to the present time been taken. It is said, that in the last thirty years the people of Canada have lost no less than $45,000,000 in connection with bank failures, and I am inclined to think that is irather an underestimate. In thirty years there have beep 29 bank failures in Canada, and in view of such deplorable figures it seems to be extraordinary that a system of government bank inspection has not been inaugurated before this. Three years ago this question was brought forcibly to the attention of the House by Mr. Pringle, then member for Stormont, and in the course of his remarks he laid great stress on government inspection of banks. Mr. Pringle stated that at the date on which he was speaking there were $600,000,000 deposited in Canadian banks, and to-day the deposits amount to over $800,000,000. I am well aware that there is a difference of opinion as to government bank inspection, and I can readily see how that may be the case. But some of the best bank managers that Canada has ever had are very strongly in favour of government bank inspection. Mir. H. S. McLeod, late manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia is strongly in favour of government inspection or of an independent audit or both, and he urged this matter on the government as far back as the year 1900, and at different times since then. In a letter to the Toronto ' Globe ' on the 26th November, 1906, Mr. McLeod wrote:
In Canada there were in existence in 1880, forty-one banks. Since then seven have been Mr. THORNTON.
incorporated and have commenced business, making a total of forty-eight banks. Of this total, twelve' have failed and some others have saved themselves by amalgamation. The failures are, therefore, 25 per cent in twenty-six years, the last ten of which were years of unexampled prosperity with steadily rising deposits-conditions under which even insolvent banks seldom close their doors.
Now, here is a very important part of Mr. McLeod's statement:
Most if not all of the above mentioned failures were fraudulent, and it is now plainly evident that a few hours examination by a skilled banker would have disclosed an insolvent condition in any one of the banks years before it collapsed.
There cannot be any doubt as Mr. McLeod says that had there been efficient government bank inspection in Canada during the last 3 or 4 years this disastrous failure of the Farmers' Bank and the dreadful consequences that ensued could not have happened, because, as Mr. McLeod says, a few hours' examination by a skilled banker would have disclosed the insolvent condition of that bank Mr. McLeod says further:
In each of the two most recent disasters a correct diagnosis could have been made ten or more years ago.
Had there been efficient bank inspection the Farmers' Bank could not have run six months without its insolvency being detected, and over one million dollars would have been saved to the innocent shareholders and depositors. Three years ago when Mr. Pringle brought this matter to the attention of the House, one of the most surprising things in that debate was the answeir which the Minister of Finance then gave on the floor of the House. Speaking on the 2nd of March, 1908, he said (volume 3, 'Hansard' 1908, page 1499):
Perhaps the most important question he (Mr. Pringle) discussed was that of government inspection. I confess without pretending to give a final judgment that my inclination is strongly against the views he has presented on that subject.
I am disinclined to favour government inspection for several reasons:
J. In the first place I think it is unnecessary. There is no condition of affairs in Canada that calls for it.
Now, if there is no condition of affair's in Canada that calls for bank inspection I would be curious to know how rotten the condition of things must be to satisfy the Minister of Finance that government bank inspection is necessary. It is most distressing to contemplate that the state of affairs existing in this country in respect to banking must be worse than it is today before they call for efficient government inspection in the eyes of the Minister of Finance. It seems to me that the

want of proper government inspection is where the Bank Act is weak, and where the Minister of Finance is at fault in not providing it. I believe there should have been efficient government bank inspection in Canada years ago. In the United States where there is a system of government inspection of national banks, a system which is not nearly as perfect as it should be, and which, indeed, is very imperfect, there has only been in the last 25 years 5 per cent of failures as against 25 per cent in Canada. It would seem to me, the Minister of Finance notwithstanding, that these figures show that government inspection is a good thing. I believe, Sir, that the time has come when something should be done by the government in the line indicated in the motion of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), I believe that the only way to get at the facts in connection with this deplorable business is to appoint a Royal Commission to make full and independent inquiry.
It has been acknowledged on all hands, and acknowledged by some hon. gentlemen on the government side of the House, that there is no other way to get at the facts except by a commission. I thought the duty of the government, and indeed most people in this country thought the duty of the government was. just as soon as this failure occurred, to have issued a Royal Commission to investigate the whole matter. They should have done it immediately after the failure. They could and should have done so. Three months or thereabouts have elapsed since the failure and nothing whatever has been done. We have been waiting for the powers that be in Toronto to move in this matter. It is a well known fact that in information they have gained there is of such a limited character that it does not throw a great deal of light on it. A Royal Commission is the only means by which the information can he obtained. The matter is of so much importance and the consequences of this failure are felt so widely throughout Canada that I cannot see why or how the government can refuse to grant this request of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). Those who have lost their all do not hesitate to blame the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding). I know the feeling of the country, and it is that if the government and the members of the government, if the right hon. Prime Minister and the hon. Minister of Finance want to square themselves with the people they will not hesitate for one moment to grant this request of my hon. friend from Halton. There is no doubt that had ordinary care been exercised when this certificate was granted, these so-called bankers would never have been authorized to do business. It is regrettable from every view point that this failure
should have taken place and I trust that the proposal of my hon. friend will be acceded to. Not only that, but I hope that there will be in the new Bank Act provision for an efficient and thorough system of government inspection. I think that the government should show its willingness to try to do something at least to save as much as it [DOT] can to the innocent sufferers from this miserable wreck.

Mr. Speaker, I represent a constituency in which there were practically two branches of this institution which was licensed by this government and allowed, with the full knowledge and consent of the government, to perpetrate frauds upon the people of the country. Many of my constituents have lost their all. At the village of Phil-lipsville there was one branch of this bank established. Across the line dividing the constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and my own constituency there was a branch located, but a great share of the business was done with the farmers in my own constituency. Many of them are stockholders and depositors, I had hoped to see the Minister of Railways and Canals in his place joining with me in advocating that the government should approve of the motion of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) and I hope that when the division comes he will vote with me in the interest of many of his constituents who have suffered, as mine have, from the fact that this rotten institution was granted a certificate by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). With the full knowledge that a fraud was being perpetrated upon him and upon the government, they granted this certificate, the minister having at the time the proof of this fraud in his hands. If he did not have it in his hands he got the information the next day. The certificate was issued on the 30th November, and next day he received a letter from the Bankers' Association telling him that the thing was not right. Why did he not obtain a warrant for the arrest of Travers for perjury? He had the declaration sworn to by Travers in which Travers had given false information, he had the proof in his own hands that it was false-why did he not act and save the people of this country from the loss of thousands and thousands of dollars? A branch of this bank was opened in Athens, adjoining my constituency. Travers came there, selected one' of the most respectable farmer's sons in the constituency as manager because he knew that he had influence in that section of the country with the surrounding farmers. Travers said to him:	I want you to go
among the farmers and offer them 4 per cent on their deposits. The rule of the Bankers' Association only permits 3 per

cent, but you will have to cover the matter up in your books so that it will not show. Early last fall, after this branch had been doing business for some time, the accountant was short in his cash, and he and the manager were'both arrested. The manager was sentenced to three years in the penitentiary for falsifying his books. He is in the penitentiary now and Travers, who got him into this trouble, will be down with him, I presume, in a few days. There is a petition being circulated and signed in the constituency of the Minister of Railways and Canals and in the town in which the young man i3 well known asking the Minister of Justice to liberate him from the penitentiary. I hope the Minister of Railways and Canals will see that his colleague the Minister of Justice does justice to this young man and has him released, because what he did he did at the request-of the manager, Mr. Travers, in order that the bank might pay one per cent more than the other banks are paying.
The Minister of Finance issued that certificate contrary to law. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said that we have a Bank Act. What is the good of having a Bank Act or of making a Bank Act if the government will not enforce it? We have a Bank Act now and if the Minister of Finance had done his duty and enforced the Bank Act this certificate never would have been granted. What is the nse of talking-are not the government morally if not legally responsible for every dollar that has been allowed to be taken from the people of this country by this rotten institution which they brought into existence? Now, they refuse to give a Royal Commission to investigate the facts. Why do they refuse a Royal Commission? Is it not patent on the face of it that some of their friends would be exposed if a Royal Commission were granted? The only excuse they can have for not granting the request of my hon. friend from Halton is that some of their friends will be exposed and they would rather that the whole country should suffer than that some of their friends should be exposed in the matter.
I will support the motion of my hon. friend from Halton, in the first place, for the reason that I think we should have a Royal Commission. That commission should investigate all the circumstances and facts surrounding this bank, and the fact that it was allowed to do business by this government. The Prime Minister, the Finance Minister, the Minister of Customs, have often repeated in my hearing in this House that they belonged to a business government. The Prime Minister brags that his is a business government. The people of Canada have elected this parliament, the members of the government are the trustees of the people, they are in the same position towards the people as is a board of direot-Mr. TAYLOR (Leeds).
ors towards any incorporated company. If any board of directors had acted for their company as the members of this government have acted for the people, the stockholders would soon turn them out, and I think that the people of this country, if for no other reason than the incapacity and laxity of the government in allowing this fraudulent institution to be foisted on them, will say to these ministers-: You have not discharged your duty faithfully, and we are now going to elect a new board of directors at the first opportunity. I, therefore, support the motion of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) calling for an investigation. If we should have that investigation and find that the government made a mistake, that they were careless in their administration, that they were regardless of the interests they were bound to protect, then they are morally responsible for the losses sustained by the depositors in this bank. It will then be the duty of the people of this country, through their representatives in this parliament, to declare that this country is big enough and able enough to stand the losses which the people's trustees have brought upon so many innocent people. The facts stated by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) cannot be disputed; and on those facts being proved, as they cannot fail to be, by a Royal Commission, it will be the duty of this parliament to pass legislation liberating the stockholders from their double liability. They will suffer enough by losing what they have paid in already and should not, under the circumstances, _ be compelled to pay this double liability. These are my views. It is the duty of the Finance Minister to withdraw his opposition to this motion and allow a Royal Commission to be appointed so that we may find out who are the guilty parties. The hon. minister says that he was not to blame, that he had nothing against the promoters of this bank after Mr. Leighton McCarthy had withdrawn his charges. But he had in his- hand a letter from the Bankers' Association telling him that there were irregularities, that things were not correct, and he should immediately have had Travers arrested, and that would have put a stop to the bank doing any further business. But when he did not have Travers arrested then, he should, four months later, when he was informed by one of the banks that this thing was not right, that these notes were being discounted, have had Travers arrested then for making false returns. He did not, however, do this because no doubt he was' afraid of exposing some of his friends. Should the commission be granted which my hon. friend calls for, we shall have all these transactions, which are now hidden, brought to light, and the parties re-

sponsible brought to punishment, but other, wise we shall be helpless.

Like many of those who have addressed the House, I have a branch of this unfortunate bank established in the town of Arkona in the county I represent. In that branch there were deposits to the extent of $43,000 besides a large number of stockholders. In common with other members of this House I deeply regret the unfortunate condition of affairs which has come about in connection with this institution, and the whole matter is a live question among the people of my constituency and one worthy surely of the consideration of the government. We have had the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) telling us that the Finance Minister had no evidence against the promoters of this bank, after Mr. Leighton McCarthy had withdrawn his charges. Well, I am satisfied that if my hon. friend had investigated a little further he would have found that the Bankers' Association sent a letter to the Finance Minister calling his attention to the fact that there had been irregularities and urging on him the necessity of an investigation before granting the certificate. My hon. friend said also that the people in the country should have put their money into the savings bank. I am satisfied, however, that those of us who are in touch with the banking system throughout the country realize how absurd it would be to ask the people to send their money to a savings bank instead of depositing it in a bank in their own immediate vicinity, and I sincerely hope that when the time comes to discuss a new Bank Act, provision will be made for government inspection, not only of the branches of banks, but also of the central organization, because that is where the trickery and rascality was carried on in the Farmers' Bank. It was in the central office of that bank that Travers conducted his operations, and had that institution received a thorough government inspection, there is no doubt we would not have had the unfortunate collapse we are now discussing. .
The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said he would approve of the appointment of a commission if the court does not do its duty. But my hon. friend knows, and the Minister of Finance knows full well, that it is practically impossible for the police court of Ontario to carry on any serious investigation. The Minister of Finance knows that when Mr. Laidlaw placed his case before the Prime Minister in his apartments in the House of Commons, he distinctly and emphatically declared that there was not one dollar with which to caTry on an investigation after the preferred claims had been paid by the liquidators.
He also urged upon the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister on that occasion the necessity of making a thorough investigation into the doings of the different men who had transactions with that bank, and he assured the right hon. gentleman and his colleague that if such an investigation were ordered it would certainly bring to the bank a large amount of money for the benefit of its stockholders and depositors, because many men would be brought to justice who otherwise would go scot free.
The people of this country have always looked upon bank stocks as one of the safest kinds of investments and have always regarded their bank deposits as perfectly secure; and anything we can do in this parliament to strengthen that confidence, which is now so severely shaken, will certainly be a move in the right direction. I trust, therefore, mat the Minister of Finance will see that before this session closes, the people who do business with our banks will have sufficient protection in that regard.
My hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McLean) said that Travers was only a tool of others, and that the depositors believed they were protected by the laws of the land. Depositors in my riding, who had placed $43,000 on deposit in this Farmers' Bank in the town of Arkona, believed up to a short time ago that their money was absolutely protected by government inspection and control, and they are to-day surprised to find that they are likely to lose every dollar, because it is emphatically stated that the only asset the bank has, after the preferred claims have been paid, is the Keeley mine. And it has been shown by the men interested in the Keeley mine that the amount of money that is owing to the Farmers' Bank at the present time is very small, and that the creditors of the Farmers' Bank need expect to get very little out of that mine.	_
What harm, may I ask the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) and the first minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would there be in granting a commission to investigate this whole affair? And will it not be a source of satisfaction to those who have deposited such a large sum of money in this bank, and to the stockholders as well, to know, that this matter has been thoroughly investigated, and that the men who are guilty of any rascally conduct in connection with the incorporation or operation of this bank have been brought to justice? There is no reason why they should not be exposed. Do the government deny this investigation because they are afraid that the reputations of some men might be spoiled? I am satisfied that if the government consult the wishes of the people who are interested in this affair, and of the financial institutions of the Dominion they will con-



duct the investigation that my hon. friend from Halton (Mr, Henderson) has asked for. If you do not grant that investigation, depend upon it, the people will come to the conclusion that something is radically wrong, and that the government is shielding somebody. The thorough investigation of this question will assist us in framing a law under which, we may hope, the repetition of any such transactions as these will be impossible in this Dominion. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) said, in regard to this certificate, that it was granted in good faith, and that in granting it the Minister of Finance believed that he was doing right. On the facts before us, we cannot come to any conclusion but that the Finance Minister was deceived by Mr. Travers and the other men who brought this matter to his attention. And not only he, but the people who bought the stock or deposited their money in this bank also were deceived. But, remember, the only men who are to suffer loss in this matter are the depositors and shareholders of the bank; the government, apparently, are not going to lose any money. Nor are, they ready to spend a reasonable amount of money so that the men who were instrumental in wrecking this institution could be brought to justice. The liquidators, as I have said, have no money to carry on an investigation, nor have they power to incur indebtedness to raise money for such a purpose. And why should we saddle such an expense upon the poor people who have been so seriously injured already? I only wish that I felt free to speak of a number of those in my own district; but I will refer only to one case. I have in mind an old couple, each about 80 years of age, who were induced to put down their names for ten shares in this bank. I think they had only half enough to pay for these shares; and to-day we find that, under the double liability, they are compelled to sacrifice their home. And these are not by any means the only ones who are made to suffer by the rascally work that has been carried on by Mr. Travers, and by the action-. might I say?-of the Finance Minister in granting this certificate. For, when Mr. McCarthy, time and again, called his attention to the fact that these men were trying to get this certificate under false pretenses, and that they were perjuring themselves to that end, it was his duty and the duty of the Treasury Board to make a thorough investigation into the whole question. This Royal Commission should be granted. Since 1905, 11 banks have quit the field of active business; five have been absorbed by other banks: one is now in process of liquidation; and five have failed. The Farmers' Bank is the only case in which the depositors have had1 a great amount of funds tied up. In other cases, Mr. ARMSTRONG.
the depositors have generally received within a small percentage of their money; but in this case it looks as if practically every dollar the depositors have placed in this bank throughout the Dominion will be a direct loss to them. The people have been led to believe that deposits especially were safe in the banking institutions of our country. I do not wish to take up more time, as there are many others to follow? My object is merely to emphasize the statement made by the. hon. member for Halton, and to say that I intend to support the resolution. My reasons are these: That Mr. Travers was not entitled to a certificate, because the sum of $500,000 had not been bona fide subscribed, and $250,000 had not been bona fide paid thereon. That the Minister of Finance had notice that the provisions of the Bank Act had not been complied with, and he did not make the thorough investigation he should have made into the facts connected with the issue of the certificate. That the president of the Bankers' Association urged upon the Minister of Finance the necessity of investigating this question; and this and the numerous private interviews that were held with the hon. member for Halton and others in regard to this important matter were surely worthy of consideration. That the minister had conclusive evidence, by the admission of Mr. Travers, that he had committed perjury even before the certificate was issued. For these reasons, I heartily support the resolution of the hon. membeT for Halton.

Here the Deputy Minister of Finance informs the general manager that opposition lias been raised to the issue of the certi-fieate. A little later on, there is another letter from the Deputy Minister of Finance, November 21 in which he writes to the manager of the Farmers' Bank and says:
Referring to your letter of the 23rd October, making a deposit under section 18 of the Bank Act of the sum of $250,000, I have no doubt that you will be applying very shortly for a certificate under section 14 to commence business. In the papers to be submitted to the Board in support of the application there is a list of bona fide subscribers of capital stock of the bank showing subscriptions to the extent of $500,000. Would you be so good as to have added to this list, for submission to the Board, a statement showing the actual amount of cash paid up by each subscriber.
Now there, I contend, was ai certain amount of precaution taken by the Finance Department in asking to be supplied with a list of subscribers, the amount of stock subscribed by eaoh, and the amount of cash paid up. There is no question that precaution was taken there. Now the supporters of this resolution have endeavoured to make a great deal out of the protest put in against the issuing of the certificate, by Mr. Leighton McCarthy, on behalf of certain subscribers to the bank.
Was there any effort on the part of the Treasury Board to find out the bona tides of these subscription lists?

There was absolutely no evidence before the Department of Finance to show that every one of these shareholders was not absolutely bona fide and that every dollar of that subscription was not satisfactory.
Did not Mr. McCarthy's letter cast doubt on it?

My hon. friend knows that Mr. McCarthy's letter was subsequently withdrawn. The supporters of this resolution have endeavoured to make a great deal of the fact that a writ was issued and a copy of the writ or the special endorsement was on the files of the Department of Finance. Every lawyer in the House knows that there is always a great deal of material put on a special endorsement of a writ, put in a statement of claim, to which no one pays any attention until some proof is submitted. What is an endorsement on a writ? Absolutely nothing as far as the case against the Department of Finance is concerned. The argument of hon. gentlemen opposite rests entirely, so far as this return shows on that specially endorsed writ filed with the department which was absolutely and unequivocally withdrawn by the letter sent subsequently by the solicitor. What does the special endorsement show? Nothing m Mr. MARTIN (Regina).
connection with the $250,000 not being bona fide subscriptions. The claim in the special endorsement was on behalf of special shareholders who wanted their subscriptions set aside by reason of certain fraud and misrepresentation alleged against Travers and other agents who had been selling stock, the fraud and misrepresentation consisting of such statements as that agents, Travers amongst them, I presume, had stated to prospective subscribers that So and So had subscribed $10,000 stock to this bank whereas they had subscribed only $3,000, and also allegations to the effect that certain men, among them Major Beattie, member for London, had agreed to act as directors when they had refused to be associated with the hank. What in that claim shows anything wrong with the deposit of $250,000 with the government?
I would have no hesitation in supporting a. request or resolution asking a Royal Commission to investigate the affairs of this bank if I could see what could be accomplished by it. But how would you get the money back to the poor depositors by holding a post mortem inquiry into the affairs of the bank?
We will find out who influenced the Treasury Board.

My hon. friend will have plenty of time to make a statement afterwards. I know my hon. friend is full of suspicion like many members on that side. I would have no hesitation in supporting this resolution if any one could tell me what good it would do to the shareholders or depositors. No good can be done by holding a post mortem examination into the affairs of the bank. I would be perfectly willing to support a resolution for an investigation into the affairs of all banks in Canada in the same way as we had a Royal Commission some years ago to investigate the dealings of the insurance companies in Canada. For instance, I would like to know some things about other banks. -I would like information as to how the Bank of Montreal came to lose somewhere between $1,000,000 and $5,000,000 in Mexico some time ago and whether they lost that money by illegitimate speculation with the funds deposited in that bank. I would also like some information with respect to the dealings of the Bank of Commerce with the Canada Furniture Company. It is generally rumoured among men with whom I associate that the Canada Furniture Company is practically supported by the Bank of Commerce. If that is the case the depositors of the Bank of Commerce have practically no assurance that their funds are being properly dealt with. I would also like to know how it is that the Canadian banks gather in the rhoney from the people of this country at a small rate of interest and immediately send it to New

York on short call loans and get large rates of interest, and what security they have for the money they lend to the stock speculators on Wall street.
Does my hon. friend know anything of the truth of the statement he has made with reference to the Bank of Commerce and the Canada Furniture Company.

I do not state that as a fact, I simply give it as a rumour, citing it as an instance to show that it might be in the interest of the country to have some investigation into the methods of the banks in dealing with the people's money. In 1907, in Western Canada, it was impossible even for a farmer worth from $10,000 to $20,000 or a reputable business man to get the smallest loan in Regina, and the reason given there was that all the money the banks had available was on short call loans in Wall street, in New York, and at that time in Western Canada we could not get sufficient money from the banks to move our crops to the eastern market.	[DOT]
To my mind, and I have followed the evidence of what has taken place with reference to this bank in the Ontario police courts, all the information the public can get towards punishing the criminals at the head of the institution can be and is being acquired at Toronto. Perhaps my hon. friends from Peel (Mr. Blain) from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and from Algoma (Mr. Boyce) who are so suspicious in connection with this matter can tell the House and the people how it was that the Attorney General's department of the Ontario government had all the information about the failure of the Farmers' Bank 24 days before making a solitary move to get hold of Dr. Beattie Nesbitt, the arch-criminal of all the promoters of the bank. I would ask them if some one did not give Dr. Beattie Nesbitt some warning to get out of the country. To show the sincerity of the Ontario government in their desire to capture Dr. Beattie Nesbitt I would point out that they have offered the magnificent reward of $200 for the production of his live body.
If the Farmers' Bank teaches this parliament any lesson it is that in the revision of the Bank Act some measure should be adopted providing for the public inspection of banks. The depositors in all our banks must be protected. This is one of the most important matters we can deal with, to see that our financial institutions are on a sound basis and when the Bank Act comes before the Banking and Commerce Committee of this House, I hope that some measure of public inspection will find its way into the Act and become the law of Canada.

The facts so far made public in connection
with the organization and management of the Farmers' Bank have done much to weaken the confidence of the public in the stability of the banking institutions of this country. It appears to me that a thorough investigation by a Royal Commission such as is suggested by this amendment into all the operations in connection with this bank would assist us in locating the weak points in our Banking Act and in so amending that Act as to prevent the recurrence of what has happened to the stockholders and depositors of the Farmers' Bank. The fact that a bank has a Dominion charter is taken by many people to indicate that it not only has a right to transact public business but that it is subject to such supervision by the Dominion government that it may be fairly assumed to be- in good financial standing. Now, section 158 of the Bank Act practically wipes out all the private banks of this country. That, section reads-
Every person assuming or using the titlo of bank, banking company, banking house, banking association or banking institution without being authorized so to do by this Act or some other Act in force in that behalf, is guilty of an offence against this Act.
The object of that legislation was to protect the public by rendering it necessary for them to do practically all their banking with chartered banks. If the fact that a bank has a Dominion charter and is authorized to do business by a certificate issued by the Treasury Board is no guarantee of the financial standing of that bank, why was this legislation passed which practically gave all the chartered banks a monopoly of the banking business of this country? In view of that, it was clearly the duty of the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board to take every precaution before issuing a certificate to the Farmers Bank. Now, just a word in reference to the name ' Farmers' Bank.' The persons who promoted this bank were not farmers. I listened yesterday to the Minister of Finance reading over a list of some fifteen names of persons who, according to the prospectus issued by the bank, were willing to act as directors were they elected as such, and among that fifteen there was only one farmer, so that about the only right, the promoters of this bank had to be called farmers was that possibly in incorporating it they were placing themselves in a position to farm the public. However, I suppose their object in so calling it was to gain the goodwill of the farming community. The discussion so far has led me to believe that the Minister oi Finance and the Treasury Board did not exercise reasonable precaution before issuing the certificate to the Farmers' Bank. We have the statement of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that he warned the Minister of Finance before the certificate was issued; we have the letter of Mr. McCarthy,

warning the Minister of Finance that the promoters of this bank were endeavouring to evade the provision of the Bank Act which said that before a certificate shall be issued, at least $500,000 of stock must be actually subscribed for, and at least $250,000 of that money paid into the hands of the Minister of Finance. We have also a subsequent letter of Mr. McCarthy, in which he gives more detail, and he says:
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it appears to me that when the Minister of Finance had this information before him he should have made -some effort to verify it, but, the Minister of Finance takes the ground that Mr. McCarthy later on withdrew his objection. As a matter of fact, that is not the case. Mr. McCarthy was acting for some half dozen stockholders in the Farmers' Bank who were his clients, and he made his objection solely for the purpose of protecting them. Apparently the promoters of the bank became -aware of that fact and they settled with Mr. McCarthy's clients, and he -as their solicitor had no further authority to press the matter. But the fact still remains that the minister had the information that this evasion of the Bank Act was being perpetrated, and, Sir, all the other shareholders of the bank were just as much interested iin the charges made against the promoters of the bank as were Mr. McCarthy's clients. Mr. McCarthy succeeded in protecting his clients but the Minister of Finance failed to protect his clients, the public, whose representative he was in that case. I say, Sir, that it was the duty of the Minister of Finance to make a thorough investigation in view of these repeated warnings, but in place of doing so what do you think he did but apply to the manager of the bank who was seeking the certificate, the man of all men who would be most anxious that the truth should not- be known. And, the Minister of Finance accepts this man's testimony, sworn testimony if you m-ay call it so, against the statement -set forth in Mr. McCarthy's letter, against the warning he had reoeived from Mr. Henderson and others, and he issued -this certificate. The First Minister tells u-s that the Finance Department -and the Minister of Finance were deceived. Well, if they w-ere deceived it is their own fault because they had every opportunity to investigate, an-d discover whether the charges made and the warnings given them were founded on fact. there appears to -have been peculiarly undue h-aste in the issuing -of this certificate. There is a great deal of correspondence about it dated the 30th November, 1906. cial reputation of this country, and no effort should be spared to place the responsibility where it belongs. Let us have a full and free investigation and base our further action upon the results of that investigation.

Mr. Speaker. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the facts and circumstances in connection with the unfortunate bank known throughout Canada as the Farmers' Bank. I do not think that any hon. gentleman in this House, particularly those whose constituencies are directly affected by this unfortunate failure, have any reason to offer any apology to this House for occupying time upon this important question. After having carefully examined the return that has been brought down by the government and after listening to the case as presented by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, I am not at all surprised that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is disinclined to grant the prayer of the resolution. The man who is being charged vith serious omissions and derelictions of duty does not display as a rule any enthusiasm for his trial to proceed, and there is no doubt that, if a Royal Commission were appointed in connection with this bank, virtually and in fact the Finance Department would be on trial. Consequently we are not surprised to see that the Minister of Finance is not disposed to grant a Royal Commission as asked for by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). The history of the Farmers' Bank is certainly an extraordinary one. The Act incorporating the bank was passed on the 18th July, 1904, and subsequently there were two Acts extending the charter, the first for two years, within which a certificate might be granted, and the second extending the time for six months. The results and consequences of the operations of the Farmers' Bank have been most serious. I think it is the most disastrous financial failure in the history of the country. It is the worst tragedy in the annals of banking. The shareholders and depositors are not the comparatively rich people to be found in mercantile circles. They, do not reside in cities and towns, and, as the notion is, make a comparatively easy living, but they are poor labouring people in many cases distributed throughout the length and breadth of the province. The savings of a lifetime have been swept away, poverty, ruin and desolation, and, in many cases, actual hunger, face those who have lost ali their means in the financial disaster known as the failure of the Farmers' Bank.
The question naturally arises, on whom is the responsibility for this failure to be fastened? Of course we all know that the loss has resulted from the operations of the bank, but the bank could not have started operations without the sanction and license- of the department, and hence the question naturally follows what facts and circumstances were known to the Finance Department or the minister who is responsible for issuing that certificate, and which should have prevented this bank from going into operation, and which should hav.e prevented the Minister of Finance from issuing the certificate. I do not intend to offer any excuse for making some observations, even at this late hour, in connection with the failure of the Farmers' Bank and giving some reasons why I deem it my duty to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). The evidence already offered before the House, both by the speeches which have been delivered and by the return which has been laid upon the table of the House, to my mind is sufficient to convince any hon. member of this House who is disposed to look at that evidence in a fair and impartial manner that this transaction is one of the most iniquitous and indefensible in the financial history of this country. I have the special reason for taking part in this debate that the transactions of this bank were carried on in two branches in the riding which I have the honour to represent, and I have personal knowledge of the misfortune, the loss, and the misery entailed upon some of the people of my riding through the notorious transactions of this bank. the government, and by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) especially, to convince the farmers of this country that that hon. gentleman took a special interest in their welfare and that he had carefully guarded and protected and advanced the interest of the farmer by the recent bargain he has made with the IJnited_ States. But I venture to say that by his conduct in connection with the granting of a certificate to operate the Farmers' Bank, in the course of its two years' operation, he has made it possible for that bank to rob the farmers of this country of more thousands of dollars than they will be able to make from the reciprocity transaction in their lifetime. I paid very close attention to the remarks offered by the hon. Finance Minister himself, and also to the speech of the right hon. It is not a defence; it is not even a reasonable excuse, for the conduct that has characterized the Treasury Department in this matter. As I view the evidence that has been offered before this House, there are certain facts that are admitted or are proven beyond any controversy; and upon these admitted or well-proven facts, it appears to me, there is no good reason why the motion of the hon. member for Halton should not be granted. The evidence has established, and no one would undertake to contradict it, that this bank has failed, has ignominiously failed, and that it has entailed loss and hardship upon some of the people of this country that no man can picture in words. I do not think that any hon. member of this House would question that that is the fact. The third point that is made perfectly clear that the possibility of bad management and the possibility of evading the letter and spirit of the Bank Act was through failure to discover a fraud. These are the three facts that appear to me to be established beyond any question by the evidence that has been offered here.
These facts being admitted, the only question remaining for solution is: Where does the responsibility and blame rest? The Finance Minister says that he is not responsible; that he has been deceived. this country who have been defrauded out of their money, who trusted this bank, say that they have been defrauded just as the Finance Minister says that he was defrauded.
