You ask me to advise you if on the papers submitted such certificate may legally issue.
Well, the deputy Minister of Justice had not a blessed thing before him, but the evidence in support of the application, and the Minister of Finance has declared to this House that these documents were the documents required by the Bank Act. and were sufficient for him and he sent these documents along to the Deputy Minister of Justice, and upon these papers submitted, which are all in favour of the application and are in compliance with the requirements of the Bank Act, he asked: Can I issue this certificate? What sort of an answer could he have expected, but the answer he got. The Deputy Minister of Justice wrote:
In reply, I have to state that the statements in the statutory declaration of Mr. Walter R. Travers are sufficient, if they are accepted.
Apparently the Deputy Minister of Justice had in some manner or other been ad vised or had heard of there being some evidence in opposition to this certificate being granted, and he very carefully guards his action, and his advice by reciting in his letter that upon the evidence submitted, if you believe that evidence he says to the Finance Minister, then you may issue the certificate. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think it is asking too much of any hon. member of this House, I think it is asking too much of the people of this country to believe that that written evidence discloses all the facts in connection with this transaction. I will not put it stronger, but I think I am perfectly justified in putting it thus strong: That there must be back of this, something that a royal commission would unearth, and which I think the people of this country are entitled to have uncovered, and the fullest disclosure made of it. The Minister of Finance said that it was not , possible now that any relief could be obtained; the certificate having been granted, the bank having gone into operation, these frauds had been perpetrated, the people had lost their money, and there was no redress. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if before he granted that certificate he considered what the consequence of improperly granting that certificate might be. If he did consider, it would have occurred to him at once that the very thing that has happened here might happen unless he exercised the care that in his position he should exercise, and unless he safeguarded the interests of the people of this country. And in view of the fact that he did not make such inquiry, that he did not exercise the power and authority1 he possessed, and that he entirely ignored or overlooked the rights of the people, I say to put it mildly, that the Minister of Finance for that alone deserves the censure of the people, at all events of those who have lost their money. Now, Mr. Speaker, I intended when speaking upon this matter to call attention to one or two particular cases which have arisen in the constituency I have the honour to represent. Inasmuch as so few illustrations of the wrong-doing of this bank have been so far offered to the House, I think I would be justified even at this late hour in mentioning one or two of these cases which

I know from my own personal knowledge. In one case a widow whose former husband was an employee on one of the railways was killed in a railway accident, and she was left with two small children, four years and six years old respectively, absolutely penniless. An action was brought on behalf of the widow to recover compensation from the railway company, and the litigation was successful, and the railway company paid $2,500 as compensation. A cheque from the railway company came to my office on a Saturday, and the widow was written to to come in for the cheque. She came in on Monday a little before three o'clock in the afternoon, and when I handed her the cheque I said: You ought to put this money in some bank where it would be safe until you find an opportunity of investing it. I advised her to put the money in the Bank of Montreal. Her answer was that the manager of the Farmers' Bank had heard in some way or other that she was getting this money, and he came to her house and asked her if she would not deposit it in the Farmers' Bank. She said she had promised him to do so, and that she must keep her word with him. I handed the cheque over a few minutes before three o'clock, and she carried it three blocks down the street to put it into the Farmers' Bank. The Farmers' Bank was closed for the day in less than fifteen minutes afterwards, and the doors never opened again, and the widow lost her money. And, Sir, all this misfortune was brought on her by the want of caution, to put it mildly, of the Treasury Board in granting that certificate to the Farmers' Bank. Let me give the case of two farmers for whose welfare the Minister of Finance is always so solicitous. These two neighbouring farmers in the township of Sydney had purchased their farms two or three years ago, paying a high price as the land there is very valuable. Last year the Canadian Northern Railway Company came along, and ran through these two farms, and expropriated the right of way, and in due course the compensation was paid to the farmers by the railway. The local solicitor for the Canadian Northern railway who is also the solicitor for the. Farmers' Bank, issued cheques to these farmers for $750 each upon the Farmers' Bank, and they took the cheques over to the bank, and it was then after banking hours, and the cash was locked up. They left the cheques there on deposit until the bank opened next morning when they were to come and get the money, but the next morning came and the farmers came, but the bank was closed and has never opened since, and the money they received as compensation for their land was stolen in this way.- In view of all these facts is there any possible justification or reason why the government ought not to grant the motion Mr. PORTER.
that has been made by my hon. friend from Halton? It surely cannot be on the ground of expense, it surely cannot be on the ground that the people of the country do not want it. What is the reason? If there is any good and bona fide reason, why it ought not to be granted, then, for heaven's sake, let somebody on the government side of the House get up and tell us what it is.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that the debate yesterday was not listened to by me; I. was absent but I have had the pleasure and privilege of reading the speeches of both sides and possibly I have obtained more good from that than if I had been present and listening. There is very little left for me to say. One of the points in connection with the matter is that the government seem to have given up their love for royal commissions. I cannot say what has come over the spirit of their dreams. They have always been very ardent supporters of royal commission until the present moment. Mr. Courtney, who has distinguished himself on one royal commission, I have not the slightest doubt, would be perfectly willing to act upon another royal commission to investigate matters in connection with the Farmers' Bank and possibly the scope of the inquiry might be enlarged so as to take in general matters in connection with the banking system of the country in view of the necessity of the new bank law which is to be brought in.
The county that I have the honour to represent was unfortunate in having three of these branches located in it, one at Dunsford, one at Kinmount and one at Lindsay. The depositors there have lost upwards of "$106,000. Therefore it is needless for me to say to this House and the country how deeply these localities are affected. I may say that _ it was in the town of Lindsay that the final collapse of the Farmers' Bank was brought about by the exposure made there during a trial which had been instigated by this man Travers. He secured the .arrest of three young gentlemen in connection with one of the banks for warning customers of the Farmers' Bank that in their opinion their money was not safe in that institution. He had these men arrested and after long preliminary proceedings the trial came on and the exposure was made showing that Travers was the real criminal instead of the three young gentlemen that were souerht to be implicated. It was as a result of that trial and the exposure which took place that the doors of the Farmers' Bank were closed.
In supporting the motion for this royal commission I do so on these grounds. The charter was obained in the ordinary

way; that counts for nothing. Following that was the issue of the certificate and if all the conditions prescribed by the Bank Act necessary for the issuing of the certificate were complied with, then the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the government have nothing to fear from the granting of a royal commission and, in furtherance of the same idea, the government are in no wise responsible for anything in connection with the Farmers' Bank. But, if the government did not take due precautions, if the government have been negligent, if the government have been more than negligent, if they have committed a blunder-and we are told tjiat a blunder is worse than a crime -then I say that it is the duty of the government not only to grant a royal commission, but, I go further and say that the people who were the victims of this failure have a very just claim against the treasury of this country for the loss that they have sustained. We find that the certificate was not properly obtained. More than that, the Minister of Finance admits that he was notified by Mr. McCarthy to investigate the information which had been furnished him. The Minister of Finance says that Mr. McCarthy withdrew his objection. Will the Minister of Finance say that Mr. McCarthy withdrew the facts of the case? What were the facts of the case? That notes were being given for subscriptions to stock and that subscriptions to stock had been raised in that way. These were the charges that were made to the Finance Minister. The mere fact that Mr. McCarthy had been settled with and that this settlement had removed his objection did not remove the facts of the case at all. In other vyords, Mr. McCarthy's statement shows that fraud was being perpetrated in a certain ease and it was the duty of the Minister of Finance to see if fraud was being perpetrated in other cases. He should have ordered an investigation into the matter. Had he done so the true condition of affairs would have been discovered, the certificate would not have been issued and these innocent people would not have been swindled. I shall not take up the time of the House further than just to present briefly this view of the case. It has been well argued all through. I support the motion of my hon. friend calling for a /royal commission in order that there may be a full investigation into the affairs of the bank with the view of ascertaining, as has been said, where these funds have been disposed of and how they have been disposed of and of ascertaining still further whether some of them may not be honestly and fairly reclaimed in order to lighten the burdens of the poor people
who are the victims in this transaction. I support it also in order that evidence may be obtained which will be of great assistance to us in moulding the new Bank Act, and still further I support it on the ground that I am satisfied that if a royal commission is granted the matter will be brought home so closely to the government and the negligence of the government m issuing this certificate will be so clearly shown that the people concerned will have a just claim against the government for the loss that they have sustained.	_
Reference has been made to the negligence of the Ontario government in not capturing Beattie Nesbitt. I may say as one who has more or less acquaintance with that gentleman that the moment I saw his name as president of the bank I warned every friend that I encountered to have nothing whatever to do with the institution. I do not see what is the cause of this government's being so solicitous about saving Beattie Nesbitt. They were not always so. Is there not something else behind this refusal to grant a royal commission, and if the government are true to their former objection to and suspicion of Beattie Nesbitt I should imagine that they would use their influence in order to secure this royal commission so that Beattie Nesbitt may be properly exposed. All the evidence that we have is from newspaper scraps, police court records and even the records of superior courts and localized references. A cohesive statement cannot possibly be obtained from such sources as these, and a commission is necessary in order to give the members of this House and the people of the country an opportunity of forming a correct con-elusion as to the facts in connection with the whole case. In other words, the evidence submitted thus far is simply scrappy. We have no systematic history, no systematic report, no systematic record of the matter at all. I shall not detain the .House farther as it is late. If the fraud perpetrated had been traced up and discovered at the beginning the certificate would not have been secured, the organization pf the bank would not have been permitted, and this loss would not have been inflicted upon the public. Let the government issue this royal commission. 1 maintain still further and I am prepared to stick to the position that the government is morally bound, if not legally, to recoup the people who have been swindled all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am very reluctant to prolong this debate and would not think of doing so but for some observations made last night by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) and the hon. the leader of the

opposition (Mr. Borden). I do not intend to discuss at all the disposition which we ought to make of this motion by our votes. In that respect I have nothing to add to what has been said by my hon. colleagues, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. I think that they both have shown conclusively that no advantage can accrue to any one in this country by the carrying of the resolution moved. But with regard to the other subjects which have been discussed, and especially with reference to the charges made of inattention to duty or negligence on the part of the Treasury Board and particularly on the part of the Minister of Finance, I want to say a word. I speak with the more freedom on that subject as I am not, and never have been, a member of the Treasury Board. I do not know the way in which the business transacted by that board is carried on except to the extent to which, in common with other members of the government, I see the results of that business in the reports from that board to the Privy Council. But with reference to the manner in which this granting of a certificate to the Farmers' Bank was carried out and with reference to the circumstances, which, it is said, called for some additional investigation or inquiry by the Treasury Board and especially by the Minister of Finance, it seems to me that the reasoning which has been advanced by the hon. member for East Hastings and the hon. leader of the opposition was pressing the case against the Minister of Finance and against the Treasury Board far beyond anything which the facts would justify. I say nothing with reference to the unfortunate difference of recollection which exists between the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and my hon. colleague, the Finance Minister, as to the substance of conversations which took place between them. But they were speaking, it is to be remembered, of occurrences which took place some four years and .more ago. . I think I am saying only what every man on this side would say with me, that there is no member of this House on either side who is held in more universal respect than my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), and I am certain that every one who heard what he said or has read it in 'Hansard' is convinced that my hon. friend felt to be true every word he uttered. I certainly do not in the least degree doubt what he has said in that respect. I do not think it is possible to reconcile the statement of that hon. gentleman with that of the Minister of Finance. All I can say is that I give equal credence to what my hon. colleague has said and I believe that each of these hon. gentlemen spoke, to the very best of his recollection, the exact truth as he remembered the conversations in question. But it does not seem to me that we need, if Sir ALLEN AYLESWORTH.
we were sitting as jurymen trying to decide what the facts may be, come to any conclusion in our own minds with regard to the difference of recollection which exists between these two hon. gentlemen, because if every warning which the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) says he gave the Minister of Finance actually took place, just as the words were repeated before this House, it does not carry the matter certainly -any farther, and in my judgment does not carry it as far as what afterwards came from Mr. Leighton McCarthy and the information given by the writ of summons, a copy of which was sent the Minister of Finance.
It is with reference, in the first place, to the contents of that writ of summons and the letters of Mr. McCarthy and the observations with regard to these circumstances which were made by my hon. friends the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for East Hastings, that I want to say a word. Most of us, perhaps every one of us, has some acquaintance with writs of summons and the endorsements thereon, and many of us-at any rate those of us who are lawyers-know something about the way in which such charges or allegations of fact are prepared. It is the business of the lawyer, when his client comes to him and instructs him to institute legal proceedings, to examine carefully the statements his client makes and put upon paper the legal result . or the summation of what his client has told him, in the form of legal phraseology, for endorsation on the back of the writ. When a writ of summons is issued, in Ontario at any rate, no verification of the statement made upon it is required from the person sueing or from the attorney by whom that writ of summons has been issued. So long as the allegations are not scandalous, irrelevant or impertinent in their character, the lawyer is at perfect liberty to frame his charges in exactly the language he may see fit to use, and I need not say that it is but ordinary prudence on the part of any practising solicitor, in preparing a writ of summons, to cover if possible all the ground that may by any chance be open to him and not leave untouched anything there may be even a hint or a hope of his being able to prove when the case comes to trial. I do not mean for a moment to say that no one should take otherwise than as serious the charges made in any legal document which may come to his notice, but I do want to impress upon every one that no one reading the lawyers allegations upon a writ of summons or other legal document is bound to accept those statements as being statements which necessarily will afterwards be established by proof, Let me give an illustration which may come home to most of us. There is probably no member of this House

who has not seen an election petition. Fortunate is the man who has not seen his own name figuring upon such a document. Now any one who has read the ordinary election petition, which is prepared by the petitioner's solicitor and which, bear in mind, is not allowed to be put on the files of the court until it is verified by the sworn statement under oath of the petitioner who seeks to unseat his successful antagonist-no one who has ever read the general allegations therein made of fraud and wrong-doing with which every election petition bristles, will fail to understand just how much information is to be had from such a document and how much confidence is to be placed in it.
The way in which an election petition is ordinarily prepared is by the solicitor-if he does not utilize some printed form that' has been given to him for the purposesitting down and taking up seriatim the clauses of the Controverted Elections Act and charging that the sitting member has, by himself or by his agents, with or without his own knowledge and actual consent, been guilty of breaches of each one of these sections. That is a much longer story than it would be if the decalogue were taken and a man were charged seriatim with having broken each and every one of the ten commandments. And just exactly as much dependence is to be placed upon what is called the ' special endorsement/ if you please, on the back of the ordinary writ of summons. I make no point of the circumstance that the allegations in the writ of summons are not verified by affidavit. I think that experience has demonstrated that the requirement of an affidavit verifying the statements in an election petition is the merest form and farce; and, although there is an affidavit there, none the less every election petition contains wholesale charges of fraud, charges of corrupt practices, charges, it may be, of perjury and personation for which, when the case comes to be investigated, even after, it may he, weeks of trial, it is demonstrated, there never was any shadow of foundation in fact. Now, when I look at the endorsement upon the writ of summons, a copy of which was sent to the Finance Minister in connection with this matter, I find in it, I think, just the same sort of wholesale declamation that is ordinarily to be found in the average election petition. It is all very well now, in the light of subsequent events, in the light of the knowledge which, years later, has become public-it is all very well now for any one to single out a few lines here and a few lines there in this long averment of wrong doing and fraud on the part of those organizing this hank, and say: Look at that; is not that a specific allegation which should have put any.. one reading it upon his guard and which was the most distinct possible warning to him
that this was all wrong? If the writ had been issued making one specific charge, I grant it would have been a circumstance to which considerable attention would have been drawn. But when there is, as there is here, literally a volume of general averment of fraud of every kind and description, I think the very wholesale nature of these charges would at once lead one to think, this is the kind of action in which, very probably, the plaintiffs have but little to go upon and are seeking by some possibility to find something illegal or wrong in the course of the organization of this proposed institution.

May I ask the Minister of Justice a question? Does he think Mr. Leighton McCarthy to be a lawyer who would endorse a writ as this writ is endorsed without having some evidence upon which he believed the charge to be established?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I may answer what I understand to be the question of the hon. gentleman in the Irishman's fashion, by asking my hon. friend from West Hastings (Mr. Porter) if he never prepared a writ of summons in the course of his legal practice that he would not be willing to swear to the truth of? I say it is an every day matter in ordinary practice' for a solicitor to endeavour _ to cover every possible ground of objection which will support his case.

The minister has asked me a question, and I will answer him by saying :	' I never did to my knowledge,
prepare a writ to go out of my office, when I did not believe I had evidence to support the charge made. And I do not believe that Mr. McCarthy would do so either.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the rules of the House, Mr. Speaker, I am compelled to accept the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Porter's) statement. Now, I say, any [DOT]ordinary business man reading the allegations with which this writ of summons is replete, could come, I think, to no other conclusion than that here was an action in which, for some reason or other-probably for good reasons if you please-plaintiffs who had subscribed to certain shares of stock in this bank rued their act, wished to get out of it. and had gone to a lawyer to advise them and to issue a writ beginning a suit to relieve them from their responsibility. That is the purpose of the suit and what I should consider the material allegation in this long narrative of charges of every kind of illegality and fraud is the gtatement that the subscriptions of these particular individual plaintiffs were procured by misrepresentation and fraud. Now that is not, at all events, so uncommon a thing in ordinary business affairs as to excite much suspicion. I have known-

and I should be quite able on very short notice to show to any hon. gentleman interested-cases reported in the law books- where men who had subscribed for sums of greater or less size for the building of a church were afterwards sick of it, tried to get out of it, brought suit to be relieved, or defended suits that were brought against them to collect. It is not at all an uncommon thing for a man who has appended his name to some subscription list, whether for shares in a proposed company, for shares in a bank, or to an application for life insurance, to seek to get out of his contract, and, in so doing, to charge that there had been grave misrepresentations or frauds inducing him to give his name to the agent who had canvassed him. That is the nature, speaking in a general way, of this suit which was brought. They have gone on to specify particular misrepresentations which, whoever sought their subscription is said to have made to them, and they have also added what I have spoken of as these general charges of irregularity and infraction of the provisions of the Bank Act in different specified matters and in further matters that are not specified.
Well, that writ having been issued, and a copy of it having been given to the Minister of Finance, some days later the solicitor for the plaintiff tells the Minister of Finance: My client's claims are satisfied, I am not proceeding further with this suit, and I withdraw any objections which I have made to your acting in this matter of issuing the certificate to the Farmers' Bank, just as you would have done if I had never intervened in the case. But that is not all. This action is disposed of by the court, is formally dealt with by a judge of the court, his judgment is upon record and his judgment and the decision do-what? Not declaring that the allegations are established, not declaring even that there was any attempt to prosecute the action to a hearing, or to make good these charges of fraud, but on the contrary, showing on its face that the action is dropped, and being dropped, is dismissed out of court. Now, do not let me be misunderstood as seeking to convey the impression that the formal judgment of the court indicates at all that the charges have been disposed of. I am not pretending anything of that nature. The judgment speaks for itself, and is quite distinct. The action is formally dismissed because it is not being further prosecuted, *because no proof is being offered in support of the charges which have been made in the writ. And the reason for it all is made plain upon the face of the judgment, the reason for it is simply that these nine or ten subscribers, or whatever number they may be, have been relieved of their subscriptions, not that they have been Sir ALLEN AYLESWORTH.
bought off, as it has been put in the course of this debate, not that they received hush money, not that they have done anything which is discreditable, but simply that some one has come forward and said:	I
will take your place, transfer your rights to me, I will buy your shares, I will pay, you back the money you have paid in, and I will relieve you of the matter out and out. That is all they wanted. They have brought the suit, they have gone to a lawyer only to be rid of their subscriptions, some one comes to them and says: Very well, you are not content with your proposed investment, I am; you have no confidence in this institution, I have; I will take your place, here is your money back. There was nothing immoral, nothing wrong or reprehensible in their saying:	Very well, that
ends it so far as we are concerned. No more is there anything wrong, or suspicious, or in any way reprehensible in the man who had handed them back their money and bought out their rights, saying:	For my
part, I am content, I do not want this suit to go any further. It may be I have no evidence of the truth of these averments, but whether I have or have not, I, having bought out those plaintiffs' rights, now standing in their shoes, and being content with the position of affairs, say that this suit is to stop, I am not going to invest any more of my money in it. And taking that position, going before the court and stating that it is not proposed to substantiate these averments, the court deals with the matter by declaring accordingly that the action is dismissed. Now, in that state of matters how can it be argued that the whole matter of this suit, and of whatever information, or warning, or ground for suspicion the statements in the writ beginning that suit might have caused to the mind of any reader, was not absolutely at an end, withdrawn, put an end to as completely as though it had never existed? If one wanted to dwell upon the letter of the thing, the suit is disposed of by the court dismissing it, that is the form it takes, that is the actuality and the substance of it. But in those circumstances I think the argument that is attempted to be made by the hon. member for East Hastings, and to a less' strong extent by the leader of the opposition, is one that is not well founded.
Now, I want to say one word upon the connection of the Department of Justice with this matter, in which some hon. gentlemen, and especially the hon. member for East Hastings, find ground for additional grave suspicions. Apparently it is thought to have been a suspicious circumstance that the Department of Finance should ever have referred to the Department of Justice in this matter. Well, I am very sure that hon. gentlemen opposite who have themselves been in charge of depart-

ments of government, would never seek to convey any such impression to the House. I will admit that when I first took charge of a department of government as Postmaster General, having as I thought, enough legal knowledge to attend to any legal difficulties which arose in connection with the business of that department, it seemed to me there was no sense in my referring to the Justice Department. I thought I could be my own lawyer, and I tried it for some little while, until.I found that was not the course of business. It is very well, I think, that it is so. Our statutes put upon the Minister of Justice the obligation, the duty, of advising other departments of government and no minister other than the Minister of Justice, though he may be a better lawyer than the Minister of Justice is, ought to be expected to take the responsibility of determining for himself legal questions when there is a proper official of the government appointed for that duty. It was the ordinary course of business for the Department of Finance to refer to the Department of Justice the question whether or not the papers which were presented in this matter were regular and in form, whether the requirements of the Bank Act seemed to have been sufficiently complied with on the face of these papers. That is just what the Department of Justice was asked for, and nothing else. There was nothing extraordinary, nothing out of the ordinary couuse of business, in the answer to the Finance Department in that respect being limited to the one question whether or not the papers which were presented in this case seemed to be regular, and whether or not, upon the face of them, the requirements of the Bank Act had been complied with. Exception seems to be taken by some hon. gentlemen to the wording of the answer which was made over the signature of the Department of Justice. I cannot remember at this moment whether the matter in any way came before me personally; I suppose very likely it did not. In the ordinary distribution of the daily business of the Department of Justice, it is only in the case of matters upon which there seems to be some advantage in a consultation between the deputy minister and myself, that I would know personally anything of a reference from another department of the government. This matter was largely of a formal character, requiring simply an examination of the provisions of the Bank Act, with the papers in question before the lawyer who made the examination, and the verification of the fact that the requirements of that statute had been met. The deputy Minister of Justice writes in reply what my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. North-rup) considers a very careful letter, as
though for some reason or other something on the face of the papers excited some suspicion in the mind of Mr. Newcombe, and he was guarding himself at the expense of the Finance Department, instead of doing his duty as he would have done if he had seen any reason in the world for calling attention to something specifically. He writes:	>
j ill-)
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 28th instant, and of the inclosed papers, being the application from the Farmers' Bank of Canada for a certificate to commence business under section 13-17 of the Bank Act, and papers in support thereof.
And then the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) breaks off the reading of the letter to make this observation:
He is very careful to repeat their question, he takes no responsibility.
The letter proceeds:
You ask me to advise you if on the papers submitted such certificate may legally issue.
That repetition of the question propounded every lawyer who has ever drawn an opinion for .a client or any other correspondent knows is simply the ordinary custom of the profession. I am astonished at my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup). It is the commonest thing in the world for the lawyer who is preparing an opinion to state on the face of his opinion, even although it is but a repetition in so many words of the letter, in which is asked the opinion, what that question is; and so Mr. Newcombe has, in this instance, pursued only the ordinary everyday practice which certainly prevails in his method of discharging the duties of his office. in taking the course which he did. He proceeds in reply:
I beg to state that the statements in the statutory declaration of Mr. Walter R. Travers are sufficient, if they are accepted, to show compliance with the statutory provisions, and that the evidence thus afforded is such as the Treasury Board may lawfully accept under the Act, and thereupon issue to the bank a certificate under section 14 of the Act.
The presence in that letter of the phrase ' if they are accepted,' is seized upon here as indicating in the mind of the writer some question of whether those statements ought to be accepted. I have not referred to Mr. Newcombe in the matter; I do not suppose that at this day he would have any recollection independently of the papers of the circumstance of writing the letter in, question. I speak of the words which he has used simply from my general knowledge of the way in which such legal opinions would be framed either in the Department of Justice or in the law office of any ordinary practitioner, and I say that to my mind there is nothing in the least degree remark-

able, nothing in the least degree worthy ot comment in the language which Mr. Newcombe has chosen in which to express his opinion. He was not pretending to pass (upon the truth of the statements in the papers that were submitted to him, he was not asked to do so, he was simply saying in so many words: That is for the Treasury Board, it is for the Treasury Board to say whether or not they will accept these jjapers as evidence sufficient to their minds upon which to act under the provisions of the Bank Act. The Bank Act does not require an affidavit, it requires simply that the board shall be satisfied by affidavit 'or otherwise' that all the requirements of this Act and of the special Act of incorporation of the bank have been complied with. It might well be that the board would be satisfied without any affidavit. They might be satisfied by the evidence of documents other than affidavits. They might conceivably be satisfied by statements verbally made, although I doubt if there has been any instance in actual practice in which the board have been satisfied without verification of details on affidavit or statutory declaration. But in this case what Mr. Newcombe wras saying was plainly, simply: I pass upon the legality of the papers, I give you my opinion that the requirements of the Act have been met so tar as the face of these papers is concerned. I say nothing one way or the other about the contents of the papers, as to that the Treasury Board is to be the judge. It may be that the board will not accept these papers as sufficient evidence under the statute; it may be that the board will cal] for affidavits from somebody else. This is from the general manager. It may be that they will ask something from the president, it may be that they will make further inquiries or it may be that they will not do so. Upon all that Mr. Newcombe was not purporting to express the slightest opinion one way or the other. The use of the expression ' if they are accepted ' simply indicates that he was not expressing any opinion one way or the other upon that point.
In reference to this whole matter-I do not mean by that what has taken place in this House yesterday and to-day, as much as the failure of this bank and the circumstances of fraud and of crime which have surrounded its operation-I can readily understand how any man, even if he were a man of very different make-up than I think my hon. friend the Finance Minister is, would feel greatly troubled under the heavy weight of responsibility, although what he did was done for the best in the ordinary course of business and in the q^ercise of his very best judgment under the circumstances as they appeared to him at that time. I can understand how, any man placed in the position in which he is now placed, after the event, when it is so easy Sir ALLEN AYLESWOKTH.
forevery one to be wise, and especially under such attacks as have been made upon him here in the course of this debate should go away with a feeling of great discomfort that perhaps if he had done something different, if he had acted in some other way than that in which he did, the fortunes and the property of many people might have been saved; but speaking for myself, at any rate, and I think speaking for the majority of the members of this House, I have only to say that I cannot see in the circumstances w'hich have been disclosed here anything in respect of which he should have any feeling of self-condemnation or anything upon which it can be properly said that he has in the very least degree forfeited the confidence which we as members of this House have always felt in him.

While my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) in the speech which he has just closed was expounding what he believed to be the law upon this subject, I could not but think of the lines of Shakespeare :
In law what plea so tainted and corrupt,
But being seasoned with a gracious voice
Obscures the show of evil.
I have the utmost respect for the legal opinion of the Minister of Justice. At the bar of Ontario he was a shining light. He brought to bear upon the investigation of those cases with which he was entrusted high talents; but I am constrained to the opinion that since he has become Minister of Justice these great talents and that bright .intellect have been clouded and warped by contact with the political souabbles of the day. We have s-een time after time where the Minister of Justice has allowed his legal opinions and his legal judgment to be swayed by the political exigencies of the matter before him. And, Sir, there never was a case in which that is more clearly shown than in the frantic, laboured and almost hysterical effort of the Minister of Justice to evade the law, to get around the facts, in order if possible to put out a helping hand to aid the Minister of Finance in the desperate position in which be finds himself. Then again, the lines of Shakespeare in * Macbeth ' come to my mind in connection with the facts of this case as we have them now and which absolutely condemn the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board. Sir, they are_the bids that will not come ouit, and though the hands which bear the blots be washed and washed and washed, and though he cry: 'Out! out! damned spots!' the Minister of Justice cannot wash out these spots lay any such specious argument as he has presented to-night. The hour is late and I shall have to deal briefly with the facts

of the case, but I shall attempt to show the position which this country and this government has to face in cxmnection with this deplorable matter. Let me say at the outset that I must confess that in a matter of such great consequence to this country and of such great pith and moment to our commercial interests, I never saw displayed swch laxity, such lofty and supreme indifference on the part of the ministry as I have seen to-night,. For the most of the day and into the night when the Treasury Board and the ministry has been under scathing criticism and charged with the most serious neglect, we have been treated to empty benches opposite, and for the most of the time not one member of the Treasury Board has been in his place. That is the kind of lofty indifference that the government shows to grave accusations of this kind, accusations of a character that have galled the government so badly that not one member of it has been able to stand up in his place and offer even a semblance of defence to the charges. And, Sir, what is the question before the House!? Under our banking laws, which we all supposed were the most stable of any civilized country in the world, which we believed were a guarantee of good faith and soundness in our banking institutions,, there was constructed this financial ship called the Farmers' Bank, which was launched upon the stormy waters for trading purposes. But, S,ix, that ship could not leave port to embark upon its trade unless it had sailing orders, and the sailing orders for that commercial ship had to be given by the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board, and before the Minister of Finance aind the Treasury Board could issue letters of marque, the law provided that they had to be satisfied In every respect that the conditions of the law had been fulfilled and that that financial ship was seaworthy, well captained, well manned and provisioned, and fit to undertake the commercial voyage for which she was intended.	But,
Sir, what of the owner of a ship who sits in his comfortable counting house and sends to sea a vessel he knows to he unseaworthy, which goes down and carries with it human lives, and freight amounting to a million or two of dollars. What of his responsibility? I put this case to the Minister of Justice: If the Minister of Finance or the Treasury Board knew that the Farmers' Bank was not properly equipped to do business, that there was the merest suspicion of fraud in connection with it, >amd if the Minister of Finance allowed that bank to go before the people of Canada with the stamp of government approval, to open its doors a.nd to receive deposits, I ask the Minister of Justice if, by all law, and by all reason, and
by all common sense that can be applied, the Minister of Finance, and the Treasury Board and the government are, not responsible for all the evil that results from the issue of that certificate? And what is the principle involved? I may be wrong in my conception of what the certificate authorizing a bank to commence business means, but my belief is-and I invite the Minister of Finance to correct me if I iam wrong-that the issue of this certificate is the stamp of government approval upon the institution, which, the moment the certificate is granted is empowered to open its doors, and by virtue or that certificate and that certificate alone to say to Tom, Dick or Harry, Martha, Jane, or Mary:	You can put your whole
fortune in this bank, and it is as safe as in any chartered bank in Canada. The Minister of Finance does mot dissent from that proposition; he cannot dissent. The sign of a chartered bank in Canada, and the opening of its doors have always been, and they are to-day an invitation to him who passes on the street to come in and transact business without any fear of being robbed. Well, Sir, the Minister of Finance was entrusted with no small duty, and no small responsibility in connection with launching this bank upon the commercial sea. The Farmers' Bank received that certificate, the Farmers' Bank failed, the failure brought misery to thousands, and a grievous cry has gone up from the oeople, a cry that rends the heart of any one who feels, a cry that can only be satisfied by this government granting that which the cry demands, a full and thorough investigation into all the circumstances attending the issuance of the certificate to the Farmers' Bank
Is there any other answer that would suit the people? Can the people be held to be silenced, can the widow who has lost every cent in the world, and the man who is unable to work, absolutely shorn of his strength, unfit by age or illness to bestow his work upon anything that will be productive of results? Shall you make the answer to the children who are deprived of their bread by this lamentable failure, as the Minister of Finance has made answer, that it is- a formal matter, a very deplorable circumstance, but one which cannot be helped? Or, shall you tell them, in the language further of the Minister of Finance, that there is a police court in Toronto before which evidence is being given concerning criminal acts in connection with the affairs of this bank? No, Sir, I say a thousand times no. Public opinion will not be satisfied until the Crown says:	By virtue of the authority
that is vested in us, there is something wrong here, we will investigate in the most concise, in the most thorough manner, every

incident in connection with that bank, and we will at once issue a royal commission. The certificate granted to this bank was granted on the 30th day of November, 1906. Notwithstanding what the Minister of Justice has said there are certain circumstances in connection with it that call for a great deal of criticism, and a great deal of explanation at the hands of the ministry. Explanation as to it is absolutely wanting and a reply to the questions which have been propounded with respect to it is absolutely wanting. The facts and the letters in connection with the matter have been so fully gone into and placed upon ' Hansard ' that I am not going to refer to them except cursorily. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice attaches no importance and argues that no importance is to be attached to the writ of summons which was filed by Mr. Leighton McCarthy. Well there again his statements bear a show of reasoning. We know that writs of summons in themselves are not documents which, outside of any other evidence, amount to very much as evidence of facts. But I will not refer for a moment to the writ of summons. I will refer to the letter that accompanied the writ of summons, and ask the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice what they think of it. At page 3, Mr. McCarthy's letter of the 19th October, appears the following passage. This is Mr. McCarthy, an ex-member of this House, a government supporter, one who gave the Minister of Finance pretty loyal service for his party, and this is a gentleman whom the minister knew, whose word he could trust and whose sincerity he had no reason whatever to doubt:
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
Apart from any writ of summons, there is a direct statement of fact throwing light on the whole transaction in writing and signed by a gentleman whose word the Minister of Finance could not deny, putting before him a charge which he could not overlook, and which the Minister of Finance never paid the slightest attention to, and disregarded. Leave out the writ of summons, says the Minister of Justice, but will the Minister of Justice leave out Mr. Leighton McCarthy? Did the Minister of Finance ever get from Mr. Leighton McCarthy a statement or explanation of that paragraph in his letter? Did the minister ever get Mr. McCarthy to disprove the grave charge to which he had appended his signature that this deposit Mr. BOYCE.
was made up out of borrowed money? Why is the Minister of Finance so silent on this subject? He has not one word to say, and he answers me with a smile. A smile! A smile ! This wreck involves the loss of millions of dollars of the money particularly of farmers, widows, old men and women, and when it is brought home to him that he received notice in writing from one of his own followers that the very conditions upon which alone he could issue this certificate had been falsified, the minister smiles!
Well, let us go a little further. One of my hon. friends behind me reminds me of the sympathy that the minister has always shown for the toiling masses as against the knights. I wonder how much money of the knights went into the Farmers' Bank, and what proportion of the money of the toiling masses as against that of the knights went into that bank? But, when it comes down to the actual, concrete question as to whether the money of the toiling masses has been fraudulently disposed of, has been stolen by virtue of a certificate over his signature, he laughs, he smiles from his place in the House and makes no explanation when I confront him with the absolute written notice that the minister had before him when the certificate was issued. I want to say with regard to the Minister of Justice that .there was a writ of summons, and that the writ of summons did make certain charges. What else was there, may I ask the Minister of Finance, accompanying that writ of summons? There was an affidavit sworn to in the high court by William Laidlaw, K.C., of Toronto, swearing to facts upon information, some of them on .personal information, some of them on personal knowledge, some upon information and belief as a result of personal interviews with some of the subscribers, that the subscriptions were false and fraudulent, and the Minister of Finance had before him this evidence, this sworn affidavit of Mr. Laidlaw testifying to these facts. Does the minister deny it? It is rather a serious condition of things when a man of such high standing as Mr. William Laidlaw, K.C., of Toronto, a lawyer well known throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and known to the Minister of Finance, pledges his own oath to-' the very facts contained in the writ of summons.
File that in the Department of Finance, put it under the nose of the minister, and it is absolutely laughed at as he laughs at the charge I now bring to his notice. That affidavit was filed before the certificate waj issued. It aocompanied a copy of the en-dorsation on the writ, and what does the Minister of Finance do? He carefully keeps that evidence from the Treasury Board. In order to bolster himself up for some reason or other, some sinister reason or other


because there is one, if not more than one, and it is bound to come out, royal commission or no royal commission-in order to justify himself he pretends to submit the correspondence to the Minister of Justice for his opinion. But in submitting that correspondence, he carefully removes from the file beforehand the writ of summons, the affidavit backing it up and everything else which would give the minister any suspicion that any one had made any objection to the granting of the certificate. Then the Minister of Finance stands up and justifies forsooth the issue of that certificate on the ground that he had submitted the whole matter to the Minister of Justice and got the opinion of the deputy minister that he could do so. The Minister of Justice differs with his colleague about the position into which the latter has got. The Minister of Finance told us that all he had to do was to look at the statutory declaration of Travers. But the Minister of Justice did not say anything of the kind, and he rather rapped his colleague over the knuckles. He quoted from the Act to show that the Treasury Board had to be satisfied by affidavit or otherwise. Well, the Finance Minister had the declaration of Travers, and he also had the affidavit and the letters from one of his former supporters in this House, absolutely disproving the allegations made in that declaration. Yet in spite of these, he issued that certificate and put the bank in the position of being able to prey upon the public. I must confess that I never heard of a minister of the Crown in a more unenviable position. But says the Minister of Justice, no importance is to be attached to this writ. He forgets, however, that there was a judgment following that writ. The action was settled, but how was it settled? It was not simply withdrawn but was settled by the defendants giving up those notes and documents which they had fraudulently obtained. Did he take any cognizance of this? Yes, he. did, because the Deputy Minister of Finance referred to it in one of his letters. He referred to Judge Anglin's judgment, and that judgment proved the existence of claims made in the writ of summons, proving that this was a fraudulent organization, proving that the deposit made with the government, which can only be made in money, was raised by way of loan, to the extent of $80,000 or mere, advanced by the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Stratton), as President of the Trust and Guarantee Company. That the money was being illegally raised was proved by the very settlement of the action itself, if not proved by the previous affidavit and by the statements of Mr. McCarthy which were never withdrawn. The Minister of Justice did not help the Minister of Finance as muck as the latter thought he would. Instead of bringing comfort to the soul of the latter,
he must have brought anguish, because he put the whole responsibility upon the Treasury Board. Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, said that this declaration of Travers could be received if it was acceptable. Then I find that the Minister of Finance has a qualm of conscience, and does not accept the declaration. Why? There can only be one reason. He has got the declaration and he says that it is sufficient under the Act. In order to bolster that up he refers it to the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Justice says: yes, it is enough if you believe it. But two days later what did he do? On that 30th of November he does not believe the declaration because he writes that most peculiar letter of the 30th of November to Mr. Travers. He wants something more than the declaration, and he is satisfied with the merest, shallowest pretense of a letter from Travers saying that the money was all contributed in cash and none borrowed. Taking the word of Travers putting himself in the hands of Travers, absolutely tieing himself to Travers when he has, at his hand so many other avenues of information to pursue. What could we have done if he had displayed that keenness and alertness which he is wont to display? I am not minimizing the acumen or ability of the minister. I regard him as shrewd and keen, and with a particularly polished acumen when ho has to deal with questions of political expediency. What could he have done? He knew Mr. Baidlaw, why did he not ask him to come to Ottawa and find out if he had sworn to what.was false? Why did he not send for Mr. McCarthy and question him about the statement of facts in his letter? Why did he not send for some of his other friends, such as the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Stratton), with whom I believe he was talking a good deal at that time about the certificate. Why did he not confer with him? Why did he not confer with the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) who had warned him about these transactions? He had only to cross the floor of the House to question that hon. gentleman.
The Minister of Finance admitted that he had conversations at that time with the hon. member for Halton. This House of Commons was sitting on that day, that Friday, the 30th of November, 1906, and all the Minister of Finance had to do was to wralk across this floor and say to the hon. member for Halton that he was going to issue that certificate that day and ask whether he had anything further to tell him with reference to it. Why did not he do it? Did he see Mr. Osier? If not, why did not he speak to that hon. gentleman about the matter? There were many avenues open, but the Minister of Finance ignored them all and pursued his own way. And on that day, in the space of a very few

hours, all these transactions went through: first, the letter to Travers saying he would meet him at one o'clock or at five o'clock; second, the reply from Travers to the Minister of Finance; then the meeting-or alleged meeting -of the Treasury Board, and the minute of that meeting; then the drawing up of the certificate; then the return of the cheque for $250,000 less .the deposit of $5,000 as security for circulation; then the letter inclosing the cheque, the delivery of that letter and the obtaining of the receipt from .Travers for the $245,000; a very hurried transaction for the Finance Minister to engage in on a busy parliamentary day, especially when the facts of which he had had notice and the evidence in support of which he had before him, were so strongly indicative of something being wrong in connection with this matter.
Now, that certificate having been issued, Travers went away. Why was there so much need for haste on that day? Why was all this thing ' railroaded ' through on that day in so hurried and unceremonious a manner? Was there a suspicion that the Canadian Bankers' Association were on to the job and were coming down the very next day? Had the secretary of the Canadian Bankers' Association not telephoned the Minister of Finance that that letter was on the way that day?

I simply say that I accept the words of the Minister of Finance that the secretary of the Canadian Bankers' Association did not telephone him that day that the letter was on the way. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, as I would say to a jury in connection with all the circumstances of this case: With substantial evidence, with fact 'linked, with fact making a chain that is absolutely complete by which knowledge is brought home to the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board of all the irregularities in connection with this transaction, the greatest suspicion arises from this haste by which all these things were done in one day which under ordinary circumstances would have taken weeks or at least a week, and done the very day when, in a city only three hours distant, and from which a letter could have been received that very day, a protest was prepared and sent from the Canadian Bankers' Association against the issue of this certificate. We have no evidence as to whether that letter, which is a very vital point in the case, was received on the 30th of November, 1906, or not. The minister has not given us any information about it. He has been taunted with that letter; and I say Mr. BOYCE.
there is a very strong suspicion that it was in the hands of the minister before Travers left for Toronto that night with the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Stratton). I say there was a strong suspicion that the minister thought he ought to get that certificate back. There was a strong suspicion that the minister tried to get it back and failed-tried to get it back and failed. Does the minister pretend to say, standing here as a responsible minister of the Crown, that, having delivered that certificate, and having received, either before that certificate was delivered or immediately after, the protest of the Association of Bankers which association is contemplated by the Act as auxiliary to the minister in his administration of the Bank Act, protesting against that certificate being given and asking that it be delayed-does he mean to say that, even though the certificate had been delivered, he was doing his duty to this.country and to the people who might be defrauded and cheated if he did not demand the certificate back? Did not he go and demand the certificate back?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Then, I ask if ever there was witnessed in any deliberative body such a lamentable exhibition of feebleness of explanation as that which has been given by the Minister of Finance;-that he did, on this 30th of November, 1906, in the most hurried manner possible, deliver the certificate authorizing the Farmers' Bank to prey upon the farmers and the poor of this country, and on that night or the following morning-that night, I believe, before Travers left for Toronto, while the certificate was still in the capital-he received a written protest from the Canadian Bankers' Association, and yet he never went and demanded that certificate in order to prevent the people of this country being defrauded by it. What explanation can the minister or his government give of that? Does he pretend for a single instant that the power of this government is so miserably small, so inadequate, that, a certificate of that kind, having been obtained, to his knowledge, by fraud

Tie having had laid before him the protest that the most highly credible authority recognised by the Bank Act-he could not go down and replevin that certificate by the sheriff, or by fifty Dominion police if necessary? What did he do if not that? Did he do anything? Sir, he did nothing towards revoking, cancelling or suspending that certificate of the Farmers' Bank. That night the minister knew, from the most authoritative source possible, that it was an improper certificate to grant. That night he had power to revoke it, to cancel it, to suspend it, to recover it. That night, the full force of this government-if necessary, the full force of

parliament-because parliament was sitting -might have been used. That night, or two or three days afterwards if necessary, a special Act could have been passed cancelling that certificate or revoking the charter of the bank for fraud.
The minister knows that, but he did absolutely nothing towards cancelling that certificate. He, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, and I suppose all the other ministers, will stand up in their places and by their vote against the motion will say that the Minister of Finance was entirely blameless when he did nothing whatever to protect the people of this country from the ruin and misery that followed his inaction. The minister will not deny that the issue of that certificate to the bank incorporated under the Act is a representation to the public that the government has put its seal of sanction upon that bank as a bank. I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not in his place; but I would ask the Minister of Finance whether the Minister of Justice assents to this proposition, that not only was it in the power of the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board, but it was their bounden duty, just as soon as representations were made after the issue of the certificate, to take proceedings forthwith, either to compel a return of the certificate, or to take such action as would render it inoperative. Well, nothing was done after the certificate was issued authorizing the Farmers' Bank to transact business, nothing was done between the 30th of November and the 1st of January, 1907, except that the bank was preparing to do business. And during all that month the bank \yas gathering in money from the farmers, from widows, from aged men, and the government took no proceeding whatever to prevent fraud. Why, in a month Travers could have been prosecuted, and have been undergoing the sentence of a court for the fraud he had practised upon the Minister of Finance. A whole month went by, and nothing was done by the Treasury Board, although the facts were plain before them. The government did absolutely nothing, while that bank was getting into position to carry out the fraud they had so successfully inaugurated. The minister does not deny that the government were deceived. The Prime Minister last night repeated over and over again that the government was deceived. The knowledge of that deceit was brought_ home to the minister. It might be a disputed question as to whether it was brought to his knowledge before the



30th of November. But after that date, a month went by and the bank had commenced to do business. Does the minister say that during the whole of that month he was powerless, and could do nothing.
I have not heard the minister say that. I wonder whether the minister will say_ it now. Will the minister say that during that month, while the bank was preparing to do business upon a certificate fraudulently obtained, it was utterly impossible for him to do anything? I hope, if only for his own sake, that he will get up and say that it is part of his defence, that during that time he could not for certain reasons take any steps to recover that certificate.

Did the minister know that? Was it not the minister's duty to look and see before he allowed Travers to be buttressed up by names of men who themselves disclaimed and complained about the fraud practised on them.
I ask the minister another question. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and I ask this House whether in its judgment the Minister of Finance was just playing quite fair with

his colleagues on the Treasury Board when he was the only one responsible to the people of Canada for what took place in this matter, that on him alone will rest the responsibility for the issuing of that certificate. He has five colleagues on the Treasury Board, and in all this iniquitous transaction, with all these facts condemning it, he kept that information back from his colleagues on the Treasury Board, and yet seeks to place the 'responsibility on the Treasury Board. He did not go to the board and say: Colonel Monroe says this, Leighton McCarthy says this, Mr. Henderson of Halton tells me this, and the affidavit of William Laidlaw says this. Does the minister pretend to say that if he had done so his colleagues would have said: Go ahead and issue the certificate, never mind the affidavits, never mind what you have been told or anything contained in these affidavits or any other affidavits. I say it was not a fair position for the minister to take or to ask his colleagues and parliament to occupy in connection with this matter.
What was the nature of the transaction between Travers and the hon. gentleman? It is apparent to any reasonable mind that there was some reason why the Minister of Finance, disregarding all the evidence issued that certificate, and after the issue having ascertained it was fraudulently obtained, took no steps to withdraw it. One is led to the conclusion that there was some motive which actuated the minister, and if not some motive, some influence. Does not the minister think that the circumstances require investigation? The hon. gentleman from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) pointed out that the Minister of Finance was not now as favourable to commissions as he used to be. He did not shrink from issuing a royal commission under the guise of an investigation into insurance companies, when the only object of it was to endeavour to drive from public life the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) one of the most brilliant minds in this Dominion. But when a royal commission is asked for now which it is believed will expose the absolute feebleness, if not worse of the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board, he dares not issue it. Dare he in the light of all the facts grant that royal commission? He dare not. I say it unhesitatingly to the minister across the floor upon my responsibility as a member of the House, that the minister shrinks from granting that commission for fear of the disclosures which may follow. The minister has had a better opportunity of knowing all the facts surrounding this matter than any other member of this House, and yet he comes to the House to make a defence which any 10 year old school boy could make. Surely the reasons which influence the Minister of Fin-1 174i
ance to hurry so much and to show himself so helpless in the issue of the certificate are worthy of being inquired into. What meetings did he have with the present member for West Peterborough (Mr. J. R. Stratton), and Mr. Travers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to be constantly answering questions and interrupting, but on this occasion it would be unfair to the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Stratton) if I should not say that I never in my life had a word with the hon. member for West Peterborough on this subject.

I gladly accept the word of the Minister of Finance, and I will put the preposition in another way-when that certificate was delivered on that afternoon of the 30th of November, 1906, to whom was it delivered, does the minister know?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was in the hands of my deputy, I presume he delivered it to Mr. Travers. Mr. Travers was here for the purpose of getting it, and I take it for granted it was delivered to him.
Will the minister, who is so fair about giving answers, answer another question? Did he have interviews with any one else in connection with Mr. Travers about this certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot recall that I had. If my hon. friend will mention any particular person I will be able to answer more definitely; but I cannot recall any interview with any person on this subject except as stated in the House during the debate.	'

One is irresistibly forced to the conclusion that there was some influence at work which forced the Minister of Finance to absolutely disregard the warnings he received, and which rendered him helpless to resist. And, after having found that the certificate was obtained by fraud, and not having taken steps to cancel it, does he not think that he should take the responsibility? Well, the certificate being issued the branches of the Farmers' Bank opened in different towns, the traps were laid, and the hard earned savings of the farmers wrested from' the soil by the sweat of their brow, poured into that bank. The money of the widow, the money of the aged, the money of the orphan, the money of the poor, went into that bank and the Minister of Finance knew it and took no action. The bank failed, and misery, ruin, and destitution followed. I say that the cry of the widow, the cry and the groan of the weary and the sick and the aged who have had their all swept awmy by this criminal negligence, is the cry that comes from the prov ince of Ontario and through the Dominion of Canada right up to this parliament and

into the interior chamber of the Finance Department. And that cry will continue, and the burden of the groan and of the destitution it carries with it will increase until the Minister of Finance and this government realize their responsibility and grant the investigation which justice demands. Look at the sort of defence which has been put up by hon. gentlemen opposite. Two supporters of the government whose constituents are affected by the failure of this bank say they are in sympathy with an investigation, ibut that because of the nature of the motion moved by the hon. member for Halton they are obliged to vote against it. There is practical synipathy from public men for you. And, there are two other defenders of the government, one from the Northwest and one from the far east and it'would seem as if the Minister of Finance had put up members whose constituents are not affected; at all events it looks suspiciously like it. But, no defence has been given to the charges, no reasonable excuse has been given for the refusal of this royal commission, and if the government desire to save themselves from the severest criticism that can possibly be laid at their doors, and relieve themselves from the reproach' and condemnation which must lay upon them, if full inquiry by royal commission be denied, they will, without hesitation and without any further parley, accept the motion of my hon. friend from Halton, grant the royal commission, and fully investigate this matter.
